title: Pennsylvania is turning data center guesswork into real, mandatory impact reports
dek: Gov. Josh Shapiro’s executive order requires operating tech facilities to disclose annual energy and water usage to environmental regulators.
body: This is the second story in a two-part series examining what shifting data center regulations in Pennsylvania mean for community transparency. Read the first story, which explores impacts on developers, here . For years, Pennsylvania communities have had to evaluate proposed data centers with limited information about how much electricity, water and other resources the facilities could consume.  Now, the state is set to start collecting those numbers from operating data centers next year — giving regulators and communities a clearer picture of what these facilities actually use, rather than relying primarily on projections. Transparency has long been a point of contention between community members and data center developers. Under Gov. Josh Shapiro’s new executive order , data centers will have to report their annual energy and water consumption to the Department of Environmental Protection (DEP), along with projected consumption for the following year and steps they have taken to protect the public and environment.  The state will also create a public map of proposed projects and give local governments new tools for evaluating them. Transparency has long been a point of contention between community members and data center developers. Residents have increasingly asked for more information about what these projects will mean for their communities, particularly when it comes to electricity, water and environmental impacts. While requirements for increased transparency are a good move, Brian Kennedy, senior vice president for operations and government affairs at the Pittsburgh Technology Council, believes these new rules could jeopardize the progress Pennsylvania has made in creating private sector jobs. With data centers comes the push to update the nation’s energy grid, which has led to more manufacturing jobs in the region, according to Kennedy.  “There are at least eight major factories under construction in western PA that will eventually produce components needed to support the modernization of the nation’s electric grid. These projects are creating thousands of permanent manufacturing jobs,” Kennedy told Technical.ly, adding, “Data centers may not create a lot of jobs everywhere, but they sure do here.” Heated debates take over PA communities Today, there are reports of more than 100 data center proposals under discussion in Pennsylvania, and these projects are “being aggressive with township officials, bullying our neighbors and refusing to listen to the people of Pennsylvania,” according to Shapiro.  PA residents at heated town halls and community meetings have asked for clearer communication and transparency from developers.   One of several residents speaking to Springdale Borough Council before the final vote (Alice Crow/Technical.ly) In Northeastern Pennsylvania, communities have pushed back on data center projects largely because of the lack of transparency around environmental effects. This led residents of Archbald, for example, to form a large grassroots movement to fight against the six proposed data centers in the town. Some local governments have gone as far as imposing moratoriums, allowing locals more time to gather information before proceeding with development. Supervisors in Hazle Township voted in June to halt all consideration of data center proposals for 180 days. Similarly, residents near a Springdale development led by Allegheny DC Property Co have called for similar measures , following disputes at public events. The new reporting requirement could give those communities something they have been asking for: actual information about what data centers are using, rather than projections about what they might use. A quick guide to Pennsylvania’s data center debate City Cast and Technical.ly break down the development surge, from energy and water demands to the potential for jobs and tax revenue. by Katie Malone Finally, some actual numbers The requirements come as Pennsylvania continues to grapple with questions about how data centers could affect electricity and water resources.  Operating data centers will be required to submit an annual energy and water consumption report to the DEP. This condition was included in the 2026 to 2027 state budget , while other data center regulation initiatives were not.  In that report, data centers will need to show any steps they’ve taken to protect the environment and the public from polluted water or air. It will also require data centers to disclose how much energy and water they use in a year, and what they estimate will be used the following year.  Data centers have been linked to increases in electric bills and were responsible for $29.4 billion in capacity charges to ratepayers, according to information the governor cited from PJM Independent Market Monitor. Late last year, the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission (PUC) called for public input on how large electricity users, like data centers, could be impacting electric bills in Pennsylvania. As more ratepayers have expressed concerns over rising electricity bills, the commission has stepped in to attempt to add clarity — drafting a plan called a “model tariff” to make large-load customers pay while placing safeguards so regular households’ bills don’t increase.  The annual reports could eventually provide another source of information as regulators and communities try to understand those impacts, particularly as more data centers come online. A new toolkit for communities The new executive order addresses the issue of transparency head-on, giving communities a new set of resources to better engage with developers.  Instead of information scattered across the internet, DEP will now be required to create a public map with permitting information about proposed projects. Meanwhile, the Department of Community and Economic Development will create guides for local governments to use regarding zoning standards and community benefit agreements.  Plus, Shapiro’s office has created a new toolkit to help local governments understand and evaluate what happens when a developer proposes a large data center project.  RELATED NEWS Pennsylvania is turning data center guesswork into real, mandatory impact reports PA’s new executive order won’t halt data centers — but it could reshape where they get built Pennsylvania exports more electricity than any state in the PJM grid. Can it innovate faster? The toolkit breaks down the potential benefits of these projects, like jobs or tax revenue, while also helping explain what resources these projects often demand, like electricity, water, land or emergency services.   It further outlines planning, zoning, permitting, fiscal and community considerations so municipalities can better determine whether a proposed data center fits their community and what issues they should address before moving forward. Taken together, the new tools are intended to make it easier for municipalities to see both sides of a proposed project: what a data center could bring to a community, and what resources it could require. A shift from speed to scrutiny The executive order represents a significant shift in Pennsylvania’s data center strategy as the commonwealth’s data-center pipeline continues to expand, making the need for concrete information more consequential. Two years ago, the goal was to push these developments ahead as quickly as possible. Shapiro initially launched the Permit Fast Track Program in 2024 to streamline the process for key economic development and infrastructure projects — making Pennsylvania one of the most attractive states for data center projects.  Governor Josh Shapiro announces Amazon’s $20B investment in Pennsylvania (Courtesy) Then, last summer, Amazon announced it would spend at least $20 billion on cloud computing and AI investments in Pennsylvania, including multiple data centers. At the time, it was the largest private sector investment in the history of the commonwealth and was welcomed by Shapiro. New permit restrictions won’t necessarily slow down developers, though. In Archbald, the Project Gravity data center applied for the required permits to start construction. They did not receive the permits, but that didn’t stop the developer from cutting down trees.  More than 70% of Pennsylvania voters oppose AI data center construction in their communities, according to a July 2026 poll from Quinnipiac University, and 34% of voters disapprove of the governor’s handling of AI data centers in the state.  “Since then, we’ve seen an unacceptable number of speculative proposals for data centers swamp our commonwealth,” Shapiro said before signing the executive order, “many of them led by developers who have no regard for local communities.”
impactSentence: Gov. Josh Shapiro’s executive order requires operating tech facilities to disclose annual energy and water usage to environmental regulators.

title: How this founder got her teen body wash into Walmart: Don’t take no for an answer
dek: Jil Ross of Chicago’s Funda Brands is learning retail from scratch. She hopes her journey inspires other women to launch their second act.
body: Jil Ross had been turned down twice when she decided to make one more appeal. The Chicago entrepreneur was trying to get Teen Kleen , her new foaming body wash for teens and tweens, onto Walmart.com. Her first application was denied. So was her first appeal. Try No. 3 got a different result: It moved forward. Walmart’s legal department asked for documentation showing her manufacturer was certified and that she had legal representation, a trademark and business insurance. All things Ross already had in order. “I’m proud that I didn’t take their no,” Ross told Technical.ly. Teen Kleen went live on Walmart.com this month. It’s another milestone in a career pathway Ross started after leaving a long-term job at United Airlines in her early 50s. Before leaving in 2017, she had spent 31 years at the airline. Since then, she’s gone to film school, made a feature film, entered retail and taught herself product development and ecommerce. Now Ross does business as Funda Brands , with products including Crimson Cloth, a bleach-resistant burgundy menstruation towel, and Teen Kleen. Ross hopes her second act can be a model for other women over 50. Friends still working in corporate jobs have told her watching her build something new has changed how they think about what comes next. And some of her biggest lessons have come from consumers several generations younger. Learning from a younger generation Ross spent 31 years at United Airlines, most of them working part time while raising her children. In 2023, she started writing children’s books. By 2017, her youngest had finished college and Ross, then in her early 50s, decided it was time for something different. After leaving United, Ross enrolled in film school through Second City, where she said she was both the oldest and the only Black student in the program. Her work eventually included the children’s web series “ CHI-nanigans ” and the feature film “ B.A.D.D. ,” which screened at the Martha’s Vineyard Comedy Fest in 2023. That trip is what unexpectedly led her to retail. The rental house on the Vineyard provided something she’d never seen before: black towels meant for removing makeup. They reminded her of growing up with her father, three sisters and a foster sister sharing one bathroom, and the embarrassment of stained towels when several of them were menstruating at once. “I’ve always wished that there was a burgundy towel that women could use when they were on their periods,” Ross said. Back in Chicago, she started looking into whether she could make one. That idea became Crimson Cloth, a dark red cotton towel designed to be bleached without staining or fading. Ross said customer research she conducted through the University of Chicago’s Polsky Exchange suggested women 40 and older were more likely to identify with menstrual stigma than younger women.  “It’s just a generation thing,” Ross said. Product reviews suggest Crimson Cloth has also resonated with adults dealing with postpartum bleeding and fibroids. Teen Kleen came later, after Ross picked up her sister’s teen and tween kids following a full day of ice skating, color guard and theater. “The funk was real,” she said, recalling her visceral reaction. She offered them her almond body scrub. They wanted no part of it. That’s when she realized how little existed for that age group; there was plenty of body wash for babies and adults, but next to nothing made specifically for teens. Ross worked with a chemical engineer for nearly eight months developing Teen Kleen, tested it with young consumers directly, and later hired research firm Verasight to survey 100 families about how they chose body-care products. Teen Kleen launched on Walmart.com in three scents: pineapple, watermelon and lavender. The teens and tweens who tried them didn’t seem to think of any of them as gendered, Ross said. Parents, however, did. “The boys who attended all the events, that was never a question for them,” she said. “But it’s a question for their moms.”  Ross is now considering a fourth, more traditionally masculine scent to meet that demand, even though the kids themselves never asked for one. That broader customer base is also why the original company name, Fundamenstrals, a play on “menstruation,” became Funda Brands. Taking advantage of entrepreneurship programs while learning by doing Ross came into retail knowing she had a lot to learn. She’s since gone through entrepreneurship programs at the University of Chicago, University of Illinois, the City of Chicago and the Women’s Business Development Center, along with the Nasdaq Entrepreneurial Center’s free 12-week Milestone Circles program. Milestone Circles gave her a place to talk through the “fires” founders deal with, trade resources and pick up ecommerce basics. “Retail was never my jam,” Ross said. Much of it she still had to figure out on her own. She learned that some brands hire outside firms to handle getting products onto retail platforms. That was an expense she couldn’t afford, so she taught herself instead, correcting course each time a submission got rejected. The business has been almost entirely bootstrapped. When her attorney quoted her $2,500 for trademark registration, Ross picked up substitute teaching work to cover it. Marketing is the next thing she’s trying to crack. Ross promotes the products herself, has reached out to chapters of the youth organization Jack and Jill around the country and is applying for small-business grants. Her next goal is getting Teen Kleen and Crimson Cloth onto physical Walmart shelves. Longer term, she’d like to build something a major consumer-products company would want to acquire. She’s also holding onto film after acquiring the rights to adapt a best-selling book. She doesn’t see much reason to limit herself to one thing. Since turning 50, she said, going to more funerals has made her more aware of how easy it is to keep putting things off. “I gave 31 years to United,” Ross said. “Let me give 32 to myself.” This story was reported with support from Nasdaq Entrepreneurial Center , an independent nonprofit improving access and knowledge in entrepreneurship to advance economic progress for all.
impactSentence: Jil Ross of Chicago’s Funda Brands is learning retail from scratch. She hopes her journey inspires other women to launch their second act.

title: PA’s new executive order won’t halt data centers — but it could reshape where they get built
dek: Pennsylvania’s new data center rules could reshape which sites developers choose, putting a premium on places with existing power infrastructure and access to lower-carbon energy.  An executive order on Tuesday signed by Gov. Josh Shapiro does not impose a moratorium, as many advocates called for, but it changes the economics and timeline for data center […]
body: This is the first story in a two-part series examining how shifting data center regulations in Pennsylvania could affect development. Read the second story, which explores what the changes mean for community transparency, here . Pennsylvania’s new data center rules could reshape which sites developers choose, putting a premium on places with existing power infrastructure and access to lower-carbon energy.  An executive order on Tuesday signed by Gov. Josh Shapiro does not impose a moratorium, as many advocates called for , but it changes the economics and timeline for data center projects by tying developments to stricter environmental and energy standards, removing projects from the state’s expedited permitting program and making tax incentives conditional on meeting new requirements. PA’s Department of Environmental Protection will play a significantly larger role in proposed data center developments moving forward.  For developers, that could make some sites more attractive than others, particularly properties that already have access to power infrastructure or can make use of existing industrial sites.  “We have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to remediate deeply troubled brownfields, including a massive fleet of former coal-fired power plants, return those properties to the tax rolls, and do it without decades of taxpayer subsidies, but time is of the essence,” according to Brian Kennedy, senior vice president for operations and government affairs at the Pittsburgh Technology Council, an organization that has advocated for the data center industry in Pennsylvania.  In Homer City, for example, GE Vernova is transforming a power plant from coal-fired to natural gas to serve a planned data center , taking advantage of Pennsylvania’s abundant resources . In Londonderry, Microsoft chose a different path, striking a deal with Constellation Energy to reopen Three Mile Island as a cleaner source of power for its data center operations. Neither of those developers responded to Technical.ly’s request for comment on how the new rules will impact their plans, but a deeper look at the new requirements gives an outline of what could come next. New agency in charge: Department of Environmental Protection PA’s Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) will play a significantly larger role in proposed data center developments moving forward.  The DEP’s job is to ensure projects align with the state’s environmental regulations. Before the executive order, the department handled data center projects the same way it would any other large industrial or commercial project. Developers were required to obtain whatever permits their projects triggered , such as air quality or stormwater approvals, but compliance with the full slate of environmental and community GRID Standards was a voluntary option to receive additional commonwealth support.  Now, data center developers must agree to a project-specific Consent Order and Agreement developed by DEP that incorporates GRID Standards before permit applications will be considered. Developers will also be required to submit multiple reports to the DEP, including an annual report on energy and water consumption and a separate report detailing the steps they’ve taken to protect the public and the environment. The DEP will also make recommendations to the Secretary of Policy and Planning for more environmental protections, including updated regulations for backup generators.  In his speech before signing the executive order, Shapiro said these data center developments must get “an increasingly significant portion” of their energy from clean sources, such as solar, nuclear and battery storage.  Explained: This is how data centers can lead to higher electric bills From surging utility demand to costly grid upgrades, several factors tie tech’s growing footprint to the steady rise in energy use across the US. by Alice Crow Another line item to pay for: Developers absorb grid costs To meet GRID certification, data center projects will now have to prove they can meet their own energy needs without imposing costs on Pennsylvanians.  This “pay-your-own-way” philosophy has been gaining traction across the country.  Southeastern PA energy supplier PECO already requires some local data centers to do so, ensuring these projects pay their “fair share” for the infrastructure upgrades required to serve them.  The Governor’s Special Counsel for Energy Affordability will now work with the Public Utility Commission to advocate for additional guidelines that require utility providers not to prioritize data centers during emergencies — like during a recent summer heatwave, for example, when data centers were knocked off the grid to prioritize residents.  For developers, the requirements add new financial factors to consider when selecting a project site, such as what updates to the grid they’ll need to pay for to make it work.  Longer timelines: Fast Track permits revoked The executive order removes all data center projects from the Permit Fast Track Program , and no new data center project will be eligible for the program moving forward.  The program was designed to speed up permitting by enlisting the state’s Office of Transformation and Opportunity (OTO) to coordinate meetings and guide applicants through the process. The Shapiro administration previously touted the program, as it sped up new developments by months and benefited projects like Amazon’s planned data center in Bucks County. RELATED NEWS Data centers could brown the landscape, or green the power sector The PA Turnpike built its own data center, powered by a solar microgrid with energy to spare Abandoned PA mines and waste‑heat recycling could make the state’s massive new data centers far more sustainable Several of the sites, like NorthPoint Development’s Project Hazelnut — one of nine data center projects that were part of the program — had already cleared several major permits before being removed.  Now, developers will have to navigate the permitting process without OTO, forcing projects back through the standard permitting timeline and potentially adding months to approvals. That change could matter when developers are comparing Pennsylvania with other states, or when deciding whether a particular Pennsylvania project can still work under a longer approval timeline. Fewer exemptions: Tax deductions get new rules Tax exemptions for data centers are also getting an update.  Pennsylvania’s Department of Revenue updated the Computer Data Center Equipment Exemption Program Guidelines to ensure that applicants are only eligible for tax exemptions if they meet GRID standards. Tax incentives have been a major selling point for developers deciding where to plant roots. Pennsylvania offers data center operators a chance to skirt the 6% sales tax on computer data center equipment purchased for these projects.  Amazon was one of the notable data center developers approved for tax breaks in Pennsylvania. At the time, a spokesperson for Shapiro said the move would benefit the commonwealth because it would “generate hundreds of millions of dollars in new tax revenue for state and local governments.” Amazon did not return Technical.ly’s request to comment on how the new executive order would impact its proposed projects in Pennsylvania. Keel Infrastructure’s data center project in Sharon, Pennsylvania (Courtesy) The changes don’t necessarily mean all developers will walk away. Some developers say they welcome the new guidelines, like Keel Infrastructure, one of the Sharon, Pennsylvania, project sponsors that was removed from the Permit Fast Track Program.  “Keel Infrastructure welcomes Governor Josh Shapiro’s executive order regarding the GRID requirements for responsible data center development in Pennsylvania,” Amanda Ignatius, a spokesperson for Keel Infrastructure, told Technical.ly in a prepared statement.  “Like others across the industry, we’re reviewing what today’s order means for our projects,” Ignatius added, “and we’re confident in our path to meeting its requirements.”
impactSentence: Pennsylvania’s new data center rules could reshape which sites developers choose, putting a premium on places with existing power infrastructure and access to lower-carbon energy.  An executive order on Tuesday signed by Gov. Josh Shapiro does not impose a moratorium, as many advocates called for, but it changes the economics and timeline for data center […]

title: Venture capital in NC’s Triangle spikes to $856 million, led by manufacturing and AI
dek: Mega deals are continuing to dominate, and investors urge founders to be selective about choosing which VC firms will back them.
body: This story was reported with support from our partner Research Triangle Park , the largest research park in North America and one of the most successful science parks across the globe. Venture capital investment across North Carolina’s Research Triangle spiked to $855.5 million last quarter, marking a huge regional boost driven by a small group of standout deals. The 2026 second-quarter total across 26 deals was a steep increase from the $183.8 million across 32 deals to start the year, according to the latest Venture Monitor report from PitchBook and the National Venture Capital Association. Seasonal shifts are normal in any ecosystem, but last year’s annual VC total was relatively low. The region hasn’t seen a quarter this large since 2024. However, the quarterly deal count was the second lowest this decade. Just five companies in the Raleigh, Durham and Chapel Hill region accounted for 80% of the capital raised in Q2, pointing to a concentrated market — mirroring national trends. “You need those splashy headline large financings to continue to propel these ecosystems forward.” Joe Mancini, Front Porch Venture Partners What drives a funding environment where just a handful of firms rake in most of the dollars? “There’s a little bit of FOMO,” Lister Delgado, managing partner at Chapel Hill early-stage firm Idea Fund Partners , told Technical.ly. “Everybody wants to go in,” he said about VC firms and investors rushing to support promising startups, “and that’s what creates this curve where there’s an outlier or two typically receiving all the funding, and all the other companies struggle to get money.” Manufacturing is getting more attention, with the Research Triangle Park -headquartered rare earth magnet company Vulcan Elements nabbing $430.7 million. Other top industries for spring VC investment in the region included AI-native startups and biotech companies, per PitchBook data.   Venture capital activity this past quarter in the Triangle region — defined in this analysis as a combination of the Raleigh and Durham metropolitan statistical areas, each measured separately by PitchBook — was more in line with investing boom numbers during the COVID pandemic rather than recent years. The average quarter saw $826.8 raised across 50 deals in 2020 and 2021, meaning investments were less concentrated during that time.  Across North Carolina, venture funding reached roughly $1 billion across 63 deals this quarter, more than doubling the $461 million raised across 61 deals in the first quarter of the year. An overwhelming majority of the cash — 84% — came from the Triangle. But only 40% of the state’s deals came out of the region, reinforcing the region’s capital concentration trend.  Similar concentration played out elsewhere in the US, with mega-deals driving Q2 investment in the DC region , Maryland and North Dakota . ‘Splashy headline’ deals help drive ecosystems, investors say Large raises attract critical attention to growing ecosystems, according to Joe Mancini, cofounder and general partner at Triangle-based firm Front Porch Venture Partners . Front Porch is a hybrid fund, meaning money is split between investing in fellow funds and directly in startups.  “I think you need those splashy headline large financings.” Mancini said, “to continue to propel these ecosystems forward.” Annual VC totals in the Triangle have dipped and spiked over the past decade. Investment hit a peak in 2020 at $3 billion across 195 deals in the region. In 2025, companies attracted $1.6 billion across 146 deals.  Local ecosystems need regional VC firms investing in nearby startups to help distribute capital more evenly, said Delgado, alongside huge investments from New York and California firms. Idea Fund prioritizes investments in the US Southeast, he explained, including North Carolina and Virginia, writing checks ranging between $225,000 and $3 million across rounds. “Those local companies will have a better time finding their way to the natural, more organic system that allows for more companies to grow up,” he said.  Individual jurisdictions in the Greater Triangle — which spans at least two MSAs and three or more counties — can sometimes compete for attracting startups and growth, but Delgado sees the region as being very connected.  “It’s like brother and sister competing for who has the nicer bedroom,” he said. “It’s the same community, it’s the same founders.” What startups should know  When founders pitch Front Porch, Mancini looks for deep industry knowledge and clear growth plans.  He also encourages entrepreneurs to be selective about their investors, advising them to ask prospective backers about past deals and concrete examples of value added. “It’s important that both sides test out for each other that they can work together for a long time,”  Mancini said. “Founders should be asking questions of investors, just as investors are asking questions of founders.”  Mahati Sridhar, a Raleigh-based partner at Revolution ’s Rise of the Rest fund, expects Triangle funding to shift toward manufacturing and hardware startups and away from SaaS. Rise of the Rest, a DC-based firm targeting startups outside major tech hubs, holds four North Carolina companies in its portfolio, including enterprise AI company Pryon . Sridhar wants to see high investment totals become routine for the region, rather than unexpected spikes. “What I would love to see for the region is it to be a little bit more consistent,” Sridhar said. “So that when we do see … big spikes in valuations, it’s not as exciting or surprising, but it becomes the norm.” RELATED NEWS Venture capital in NC’s Triangle spikes to $856 million, led by manufacturing and AI Technical.ly launches reporting series on North Carolina’s Research Triangle: Tell us your story From greenhouse roots to gene editing: How Shai Lawit found his agtech calling
impactSentence: Mega deals are continuing to dominate, and investors urge founders to be selective about choosing which VC firms will back them.

title: Robot safety startup FORT Robotics sets sights on going public in $556M deal
dek: The Philadelphia company plans to list on the Nasdaq via a SPAC merger, marking the region’s second major robotics exit announcement this year.
body: FORT Robotics is taking Philly’s growing robotics momentum to Wall Street. The startup, which makes safety tech for robots and autonomous machines, announced plans to go public today at a $556 million valuation. Instead of a traditional IPO, FORT plans to combine with special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) Newbury Street II Acquisition Corp, already listed on the Nasdaq. Once the two companies come together, the business will be known as FORT Robotics Holdings and is expected to trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol FROB. The deal will support the company’s continued product development. “FORT’s mission is to ‘ensure robots cause no harm’,” founder and CEO Samuel Reeves said in a press release . “We are dedicated to pioneering and building a shared framework for trust that robot manufacturers, integrators, end users, regulators, insurers, governments and any other interested party can rely on.”  SPACs are an alternate route to the public markets, in which a private company combines with an already-public shell company. A startup may go that route because it can offer a faster and more predictable way to reach the public markets than a traditional IPO. FORT did not immediately respond to Technical.ly’s request for comment. Founded in 2018, the startup spun out of Humanistic Robotics , which made safety devices for landmines.  Since then, FORT has grown its robotics safety systems and raised multiple larger funding rounds, including a $13 million Series A backed in part by Mark Cuban and a $25 million Series B . Last summer, it added almost $19 million to that funding round to support expansion of its platform.  Earlier this year, FORT acquired Pittsburgh-based autonomous vehicle software startup Mapless AI , adding Mapless’ remote teleoperation capabilities to its safety system, the Trust Platform.  FORT’s news marks the second Philly robotics company that announced plans to go public this year. Penn spin-out Exyn Technologies, which builds software to help drones and other robots move through difficult spaces on their own, announced plans to IPO in May.
impactSentence: The Philadelphia company plans to list on the Nasdaq via a SPAC merger, marking the region’s second major robotics exit announcement this year.

title: Inside the room-by-room battle to enforce Maryland’s classroom cellphone bans
dek: A statewide mandate left teachers without funding or support to police mobile devices, turning policy into a daily struggle.
body: For veteran 12th-grade English teacher Lee Krempel, Baltimore City’s recent cellphone ban delivered a brief taste of “teaching heaven.” Then came the burner phones. “For the first time in years,” Krempel said of the first three months of enforcement, “I’d look up and no students were looking down at their phones — just a completely different world of teaching.” “It felt like building sand castles on the shoreline.” Lee Krempel, Baltimore City schools Once winter break hit, the bliss was over. Instead of turning in their actual phones for locker storage, students brought old ones, keeping true devices close to their chests. What began as a unified administrative front soon became a room-by-room battle waged by individual teachers, Krempel said. By the end of the school year, the dropped heads and glazed-over eyes of previous years had returned. Krempel’s experience captures the gap between Maryland’s cellphone ban on paper and one that actually works in a classroom. At least 39 states have adopted similar restrictions — often, as six teachers told Technical.ly, under the weight of limited funding, absent district backup and impossible logistics. “It felt like building sand castles on the shoreline,” Krempel said. “There’s a kind of entropy that happens when you’re doing a policy like this. Over the course of time, it just wears away.” A seemingly simple policy quickly became a logistical puzzle for the people charged with enforcing it. Piling onto teachers’ plates As a new Baltimore City Schools teacher in 2017, Khadim Baluch was eager to integrate technology into the classroom. When his high school couldn’t afford enough laptops for students, he adapted by incorporating cellphones into his lesson plans. The strategy backfired. Phones fractured student focus and degraded classroom culture, Baluch said. A 2024 Pew Research Center survey found that 72% of US high school teachers considered cellphone distraction a major problem in their classrooms . Now a Baltimore middle school administrator, Baluch welcomed the cellphone ban, which launched districtwide in August 2025. Like others, implementation initially went well, with students storing devices in their lockers.  But a new district directive requires middle schoolers to adopt the high school protocol, handing their phones directly to teachers upon arrival — an additional responsibility for an already overworked group.   “The job of a teacher is already incredibly overwhelming,” Baluch said. “Now, you’re responsible for 35 students’ $1,000 devices — without any way to secure them?” A high school educator in Prince George’s County told Technical.ly that administrators are hesitant to ask teachers to collect phones because parents have complained.  The teacher, who requested their name be withheld for fear of administrative pushback, is considering spending $400 of their own money on a phone lockbox — both to enforce restrictions and to ensure no devices go missing. “It’s just another thing I have to pay for out of my pocket,” they said.  Maryland’s cellphone law came with directives, but no dedicated state funding to implement them, leaving schools to figure out the logistics with existing resources.  Yondr pouches (Courtesy) In 2024, several schools in Baltimore County paid for a strategy beyond standard locker storage: Yondr pouches.  A hallway monitor walked the building carrying the magnetic, lockable pouches for students who couldn’t keep their phones put away, Sam Hurd, a middle school teacher, said. “Those became a big hassle,” Hurd said. “Students just found a way to break into them.” A statewide mandate, a local enforcement problem Maryland’s law leaves districts to decide how the ban should be enforced. Krempel said his school initially took a strong approach, but teachers were increasingly left to enforce the policy themselves. “There seems to be a lack of willingness,” Krempel said, “to have a really strong hand about it at the district level.” Finding an appropriate disciplinary response is tricky, particularly given Maryland’s law prohibiting suspensions and expulsions for cellphone violations. That leaves schools with a narrower set of tools for enforcing the policy. Despite restrictions, a district spokesperson told Technical.ly that late 2025 survey results showed staff generally understood and smoothly enforced the policy, though high school teachers did report unique challenges on their campuses. It’s a concern shared nationwide, with 60% of high school educators reporting that cellphone policies are difficult to enforce, according to a Pew Research study.  “We are working with our schools to incorporate strategies to address the lessons learned as we build on the overall successful first-year implementation,” a City Schools spokesperson wrote in an email, “and work towards enhancing effectiveness for the 2026-2027 school year.” Teaching students to sit with the discomfort At Hurd’s middle school in Baltimore County, the cellphone ban eventually became less of a fight.  Most teachers and administrators now enforce the rules consistently, he said, using lunch detention or calls home for repeat violations. Getting students to follow the rules is different from making them want their phones less, but Hurd has noticed students’ increasing awareness of how devices affect their learning and mental health. “They’re more aware of the destructive habits they form with a phone,” Hurd said, “yet they’re wholly unwilling to part with it.” City Schools’ Krempel is taking a different approach. In his mindfulness club, he asks students to confront what happens when they’re separated from their phones . For Krempel, that may be the harder lesson — and the one no statewide policy can enforce. “When they feel fidgety without their phones, we take a moment and do a breath exercise,” Krempel said. “Learning to experience that discomfort and boredom.”
impactSentence: A statewide mandate left teachers without funding or support to police mobile devices, turning policy into a daily struggle.

title: For Kenya Porter, Pittsburgh’s tech future is personal
dek: The founder of Explore PGH Tech Week, which returns Sept. 10-16, has a long relationship with the city’s innovation scene — going all the way back to her grandfather.
body: This is a guest post by Orlana Darkins Drewery , communications lead for Explore Pittsburgh Tech Week , happening Sept. 10-16, 2026. Technical.ly is a media partner. When Kenya Porter walks across Carnegie Mellon University’s campus, she sometimes sees more than one of the world’s most recognized centers of technology and innovation. She sees her grandfather. In the 1960s and early 1970s, Porter’s grandfather worked as a chauffeur for Paul Cross, the president of the Mellon Institute, which later merged with Carnegie Institute of Technology to form the university we know today as Carnegie Mellon University. His employment created an educational opportunity for his children, opening a door to an institution that, at the time, would have felt out of reach for many Black families. “Every time I’m on [the CMU] campus, I can almost see my grandfather leaning against a car, waiting for the president to come out.” Kenya Porter, Explore Pittsburgh Tech Week Porter’s uncle, Audie Stokes, walked through that door. He graduated from Carnegie Mellon in 1976 with a degree in math and another in civil engineering, a significant accomplishment for a Black man entering the engineering field during that era. Her mother’s story was different. She attended Avalon High School with a graduating class of 56 students. Although she was among the top 10 students in her class, the percentage-based eligibility requirement put the opportunity to attend Carnegie Mellon just beyond her reach. Decades later, Porter found herself walking onto that same campus under very different circumstances. She had been invited to serve on the planning committee for Carnegie Mellon’s Startup PGH , helping contribute to conversations about Pittsburgh’s entrepreneurial tech and innovation ecosystem. “It was very emotional for me,” Porter said. “Every time I’m on that campus, I can almost see my grandfather leaning against a car, waiting for the president to come out.” For Porter, the moment represented more than professional recognition. It connected three generations of her family to a larger question that has followed her throughout her career. That question is also at the heart of Explore Pittsburgh Tech Week , the citywide technology and innovation week Porter founded and now produces through her company, Explore Innovations . Bringing tech to Pittsburgh’s K-12 students Porter’s path to founding Explore was built through more than a decade of work spanning technology, financial services, city infrastructure, product and program management and operations. At PNC Financial Services, she rose to Assistant Vice President and Senior CX Product Manager. She later joined Google as an Engineering Program Manager, where her work included helping lead and scale products and features such as YouTube Shorts, Reserve with Google and the quality and data infrastructure supporting the Google Shopping experience. But some of the work that would have the greatest influence on Porter’s vision for Pittsburgh happened outside her formal job responsibilities. As Google’s K-12 Pittsburgh lead, an executive volunteer role, Porter helped bring hundreds of Pittsburgh students into Google’s local offices each year. Students learned coding, toured the workplace and heard directly from Googlers about the paths that led them into technology careers. While at PNC, she was voted in and served as the president of the African American EBRG serving over 1,000 employees, another volunteer executive role, creating professional development workshops and experiences for PNC employees.  She also helped integrate the Google IT Certification into Pittsburgh Public Schools at no cost to students and launched a formal mentorship program through the K-12 initiative. Those experiences reinforced something Porter had already learned through her own family’s history: Sometimes people need more than information about an opportunity. They need access to the room. That thinking eventually helped shape Explore Pittsburgh Tech Week . Now in its third year, the week returns Sept. 10 through 16, presented by Google. More than 20 activations across Pittsburgh will bring together students, entrepreneurs, educators, employers, workforce professionals and technologists around artificial intelligence, workforce development, entrepreneurship, education, health and other areas influencing the region’s future. ‘Where tech meets community’: More than just a tagline For Porter, the week’s tagline phrase reflects a larger challenge facing a city internationally recognized for artificial intelligence, robotics, research and advanced technology. Pittsburgh has the institutions. It has researchers, companies, universities and talent. The question is whether enough Pittsburghers can see themselves as part of what is being built. Porter believes the next chapter of Pittsburgh’s technology economy cannot be measured only by companies launched, investments secured, or innovations developed. Its success will also depend on how many people can find a path into that economy , including students and workers who may never have considered themselves part of the technology community . That makes Explore more than a week of programming for its founder. In many ways, it is personal. Her grandfather drove the car. Her uncle earned two degrees. And generations later, Porter is returning to some of those same institutions, this time as a leader, partner and builder working to widen the path for others. “I feel that I’m literally standing on my ancestors’ shoulders,” Porter said. Perhaps that is why walking across Carnegie Mellon’s campus still carries so much weight for her. She walks across the campus her mother couldn’t.  She can picture her grandfather standing beside that car. Only now, his granddaughter has a seat at the table. Explore Pittsburgh Tech Week 2026 takes place Sept. 10-16. Learn more and register for events at TechWeekPittsburgh.com .
impactSentence: The founder of Explore PGH Tech Week, which returns Sept. 10-16, has a long relationship with the city’s innovation scene — going all the way back to her grandfather.

title: Rules for human writing in the AI age
dek: The world is busy writing rules for the machines. These are for the people who still write — like Technical.ly does.
body: AI has no place in writing poetry. It does have a big role in journalism. I came to my reporting career from an interest in creative writing first. I only later became a devotee to informing communities. So I have several rolling conversations with friends about what this era of generative AI means for something I’ve loved for as long as I can remember: assembling words in a particular order to create meaning for others. Tech-forward friends tease me that my life’s work is being automated away. Writer friends joke that I’m crossing the picket line by even entertaining how this era’s new tools could fit into my practice. Lots of problems come with any big paradigm shift, and artificial intelligence is no different. As a news organization that employs human writers and community reporters, Technical.ly has plenty of internal debate. Our coverage remains open to good-faith perspectives across the spectrum, but I believe it’s unlikely that we will ever again hire someone who is opposed to the technologies across the board (as opposed to particular uses and models).  Lots of problems come with any big paradigm shift, and artificial intelligence is no different. Early on, Technical.ly established our own ethics policy for AI usage , and it will continue to evolve. More recently, I got into a conversation with Danya Henninger, the Technical.ly editorial director overseeing our newsroom, about what defining rules are worth following when engaging AI for writing. To me as someone who will likely always identify as a writer, I draw a bright line between different types of writing I do for different reasons. I do write poetry. I still create stories and order words with intention. AI never really comes to mind in those uses — it breaks the whole goal I have. These words in this essay were all written like I’ve written for decades, as a stream of consciousness and then tightened with an edit.  But my journalistic practice is something different. My first goal is not my enjoyment or self-discovery; My journalistic priority is to inform a community to the best of my ability. I routinely rely on a suite of AI tools for research, fact-checking and data analysis. I still write plenty, because I believe part of our distinction is that we’re real people.  Still, I wanted to share a few rules I follow, beyond ethics, and more to good writing when a generative AI tool lurks somewhere near.  Below, I humbly submit those I follow in the hopes you’ll follow them too. I’d love to hear your own. Writing done faster is rarely done better. Use AI to make your writing truer — not easier. AI writes in math. Your job is to translate it back into natural language. Infuse your work with what AI can’t: personal experience, perspective, passion. Practice omission and restraint. Prefer one em dash to three, and limit the triads. Read every line aloud. If you skip over your words, so will your reader.
impactSentence: The world is busy writing rules for the machines. These are for the people who still write — like Technical.ly does.

title: Cattle tech spurs North Dakota VC uptick: $16.3M raised in spring quarter
dek: Fargo-based agtech firm 701x accounted for more than 60% of the state’s quarterly VC investment, but regional leaders say broader strategy matters more than totals.
body: One large agtech financing drove an uptick in North Dakota venture investment this spring, boosting the quarterly statewide funding from $3 million in Q1 to $16.3 million in Q2. The most recent quarter, April to June, included four North Dakota deals, according to the latest PitchBook-National Venture Capital Association Venture Monitor report. In the first half of the year, North Dakota recorded $19M in VC deals, up 66% from lackluster 2025. In the first half of 2026, North Dakota recorded $19.3 million across six deals , up 66% from $11.6 million across six deals during the same period last year. While the increase is notable, 2025 marked a significant low point after several years where North Dakota’s annual venture investment regularly topped $100 million.  Kodee Furst, a director at 50 South Capital , which manages the North Dakota Growth Fund , believes completed venture deals are only one measure of the state’s startup economy. “Venture capital data tells an important part of the story, but it’s only one measure of a much broader strategy,” Furst said to Technical.ly. “The work happening across founder support, talent, partnerships and capital formation is expanding North Dakota’s capacity to produce more high-growth companies for years to come.” One agtech round drove most of Q2 Fargo-based cattle technology company 701x raised a $10 million Series B in June, accounting for about 61% of the total raised by all North Dakota’s startups in the second quarter. The round was funded entirely by individual investors, according to a 701x press release, including North Dakotans, Minnesotans and ranchers around the country who use its products. No venture capital firms or institutional investors participated. “Closing an oversubscribed round funded by our neighbors, our community, and our own customers is the kind of validation that means the most to us,” 701x CEO Kevin Biffert said in the release.  Why did a $673M deal disappear from PitchBook’s North Dakota data? While reviewing North Dakota’s historical venture data, we spotted something that didn’t look right: PitchBook showed a $673.18 million financing for Fargo-based Edgewood Properties in Q4 2025. That single transaction would have dwarfed nearly every other venture deal in the state — not just in that quarter, but in all recent recorded history.  PitchBook’s company profile for Edgewood showed a clue. Between 2018 through 2024, it listed nine different capital raises, and they added up to exactly $673.18 million. What happened? Well, in October 2025, the company added all nine together in one update, filing something called a Form D amendment with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. Technical.ly asked PitchBook about the discrepancy.  After reviewing the underlying filings, PitchBook’s Data Operations team determined that the $678M did, in fact, represent eight years of raises. PitchBook said it often treats Form D amendment filings like this, as tranches of a single fundraising round. But in most cases, tranched rounds happen over several months rather than several years, so it doesn’t cause an issue. After Technical.ly pointed out what happened, PitchBook redistributed Edgewood’s financing activity across 2018 through 2024, when the individual tranches actually occurred. The correction substantially changed North Dakota’s historical venture totals. PitchBook’s original data showed about $692.1 million invested in the state in 2025, including roughly $679.7 million in Q4 alone. Adjusting the Edgewood amount reduced the full-year total to about $19 million and Q4 to about $6.5 million. This is a reminder that a single misclassified deal can dramatically distort the picture — and that reporters here at Technical.ly will always question when the numbers don’t look right. The company, which makes smart ear tags and herd-management software for cattle producers, also said it had achieved its first profitable month and was accelerating an international expansion. The other three transactions were spread across insurance, agriculture and business products. PitchBook records a $4 million financing for Grand Forks-based Tugboat Solutions , an insurtech company that helps homeowners navigate property insurance claims. Tugboat publicly announced the financing as a $3 million seed round, led by Resilience VC with participation from South Dakota First, gener8tor, Sure Ventures, Acumen, 701 Fund and other investors. Lilac Agriculture , an NDSU spinout developing microbial crop inoculants, accounted for another $1.68 million. The fourth deal was a $601,500 financing for Hoefer Group , a Dunseith company developing lightweight recreational vehicles. Together, the three largest deals accounted for more than 96% of the quarter’s capital.  “It continues to be encouraging to see regional startups and growth stage companies closing capital rounds,” John Machacek, chief innovation officer at the Greater Fargo Moorhead Economic Development Corporation, told Technical.ly. North Dakota mirrored national venture trends in one important way: A small number of transactions drove an outsized share of investment. But the industries receiving that money looked very different. Across the US, PitchBook recorded about $144.9 billion in venture investment in Q2. Anthropic’s $65 billion financing alone represented nearly 45% of the national quarterly total. While AI dominated the largest national deals, North Dakota’s Q2 funding was concentrated in agriculture-related companies: 701x and Lilac accounted for nearly three-quarters of the state’s venture investment. What the data doesn’t show The four completed deals are only one piece of North Dakota’s broader effort to increase the number of companies capable of attracting outside investment. Furst, of 50 State Capital, said the North Dakota Growth Fund has spent the past five years focused on building long-term capacity, rather than judging the ecosystem by individual funding rounds or particularly strong years. The fund was created in 2021, when the State Investment Board committed $100 million from North Dakota’s Legacy Fund, a pre-existing fund built from oil and gas tax revenue.  An additional $150 million commitment in 2025 brought the Growth Fund to $250 million. Under 50 State’s management, the fund invests in companies and private funds with ties to North Dakota across venture capital, growth equity, private credit and other private-market strategies. It’s one of a collection of state resources, noted Machacek of the Greater Fargo Moorhead EDC. He cited the North Dakota Development Fund , LIFT , Innovate ND , the Angel Match Program and Bank of North Dakota . “This enhances the financial tool chest,” Machacek said. Gener8tor, a startup accelerator and VC firm that operates in several US cities, expanded into North Dakota in 2022 through a partnership with 50 South Capital. Its North Dakota investment accelerator offers $100,000 investments to five startups per cohort, along with 12 weeks of mentorship and investor connections. Its gBETA programs in Fargo and Grand Forks provide free, non-equity support to earlier-stage companies. That kind of work can happen months or years before a company closes a round that appears in PitchBook, Furst noted, while founders are developing products, finding customers and preparing to approach investors. “Durable innovation ecosystems aren’t created by a single funding round or one exceptional year of venture investment,” Furst said. “They are built by consistently expanding the number of entrepreneurs, companies and investors participating in the market, and we believe the fund investments made to date will continue to translate into stronger venture outcomes over time.”
impactSentence: Fargo-based agtech firm 701x accounted for more than 60% of the state’s quarterly VC investment, but regional leaders say broader strategy matters more than totals.

title: Hillman Foundation grant backs TiE Pittsburgh’s effort to connect local startups with global VCs
dek: Executive Director Alex Dalton is partnering with the region’s robotics network to bring outside investors to town during StartUP Week.
body: A $25,000 grant from the Hillman Foundation is fueling a new push to address one of Pittsburgh’s thorniest tech challenges: bringing global venture capital to local startups. The Southwestern PA-based philanthropic funder awarded the grant to Alex Dalton , executive director of TiE’s Pittsburgh chapter, who is now compiling a list of promising companies to pitch to the broader organization’s global investor network. “There’s lots of activities that you can do to activate local capital, and sure we will continue to try and do those things,” Dalton told Technical.ly, “but I do really think one of the big missing things for this ecosystem is the connection to the external markets in a meaningful way — a meaningful bridge for those founders who might not know how to reach it.”  Alex Dalton (Courtesy) TiE has more than 60 regional chapters in over a dozen countries, with some 4,000 charter members who are also active investors, according to Dalton.  Pittsburgh founders have long cited access to external capital as a major barrier to building a successful startup in the ecosystem. While the $25,000 grant isn’t directly available as a source of funding for startups, Dalton says building out the network will ultimately lead to more connections and, eventually, investments for early-stage founders.  Dalton plans to host outside and local TiE charter members during Pittsburgh’s Tech and StartUP week (Sept. 10 to 18), offering tours of local robotics labs and Discovery Day , as well as facilitating connections to local companies.  “If we can build something around this and do it for the next 10 years, I think that is how you begin to move the needle for an ecosystem like Pittsburgh,” Dalton said.   Dalton, a 2026 RealLIST Connector and startup founder himself, is partnering with the Pittsburgh Robotics Network on this project, which they’ve jointly dubbed “Robocon.”  Early-stage robotics founders who would like to connect with TiE’s investor network can email Dalton at ed@tiepgh.org. Founded in 1992, TiE has had a Pittsburgh presence since 2001. The organization played an active role in ecosystem building in Pittsburgh during the early 2000s, according to Dalton, but its influence has waned in recent years.  Dalton said he’s been working to change that. Since assuming the executive director role in 2023, he’s been ramping up TiE Pittsburgh’s Open Mic Nights, an event series for local founders, researchers, students and technologists to give short talks about their work.  “I really think that this [funding] is a signal from the Hillman Foundation, as well as the ecosystem,” Dalton said, “that TiE is ready to be impactful again.”
impactSentence: Executive Director Alex Dalton is partnering with the region’s robotics network to bring outside investors to town during StartUP Week.

title: Everybody loves New Orleans. Why doesn’t Louisiana?
dek: Despite ranking among America’s favorite metros, the city is shrinking rapidly while political friction with Baton Rouge stalls a turnaround.
body: • New Orleans ranks No. 7 among the 50 largest US cities in YouGov’s second-quarter 2026 popularity data, viewed favorably by 58% of Americans placing it in top-tier company alongside Nashville and Boston. • After years of decline, Louisiana’s population has returned to modest growth, yet New Orleans continues to shrink. • Local leaders have a plan to reverse it that will need state support — but the state keeps treating its most beloved city as a problem to manage. The country keeps falling for New Orleans. Fresh polling ranks it the No. 7 most popular of America’s 50 largest cities, viewed favorably by 58% of Americans — the kind of company usually reserved for San Francisco and Boston. By YouGov’s net-favorability measure , only a handful of US cities beat it.  Yet the people who know it best keep leaving. New Orleans is now the fastest-shrinking major metro in the country. The city has fallen to about 363,000 residents (roughly 100,000 below its pre-Katrina peak), declining for the fourth time in five years.   America adores a city its own state seems to regard as a problem to be managed. The city’s economic development org GNO Inc. is prioritizing population reversal too , the group’s chief Michael Hecht told Axios last month. Given the widespread love for New Orleans, still the state’s biggest city, one might think it would be central to the state’s own strategy. That’s less clear.  Consider how Louisiana’s leaders treat the asset. In September 2025, Gov. Jeff Landry asked the Pentagon for up to 1,000 National Guard troops to help patrol New Orleans and two other cities, citing violent crime. The timing was strange: the city was closing out its safest year in half a century, on pace for its fewest killings in more than five decades.  Louisianans themselves seem to grasp the city’s real value better than that posture suggests.  In the 2025 Louisiana Survey from LSU’s Reilly Center, residents said crime hurts the state’s tourism far more than it threatens their own safety — roughly a third called the impact on tourism “a great deal,” versus about a fifth who said the same of their personal safety.  They’re not saying they feel unsafe. They’re saying they’re worried about their reputation. So why the friction? Notably, yes, it’s politics.  A city at odds with its home state New Orleans is Louisiana’s Democratic heart in a state that has moved hard the other way.  Orleans Parish gave 82% of its vote to Kamala Harris in 2024, while Louisiana went about 60% for Donald Trump ,  one of the country’s largest gaps between a big city and its home state. That gap shows up in law: Louisiana is a so-called “Dillon’s Rule” state, which means local governments only have power given to them by the state. In turn, the legislature has repeatedly preempted the city’s local authority on matters from firearms to labor standards. It shows up in policing, where Landry stood up a dedicated state police unit for the city before reaching for the Guard.  The distrust isn’t invented. New Orleans has handed the rest of the state real reasons for skepticism. Infamously a mayor went to federal prison for taking more than $500,000 in bribes. A city with that record shouldn’t be shocked when Baton Rouge keeps a hand on the wheel. But skepticism is not a strategy, and treating your most valuable asset as a liability carries a cost, especially when that asset is losing people.  The states that compound their advantages lean into a marquee city rather than fight it: Nashville and Austin, both all well-liked cities, contribute meaningfully to Tennessee and Texas respectively, despite their own political and cultural differences.   A superpower, not a burden A city the country already loves does work no marketing budget can buy. It pulls in workers, founders, students — exactly the people New Orleans is currently bleeding. This fall, hundreds of economic development leaders from around the world will attend thei r annual conference i n much beloved New Orleans. State leaders say they have a strategy to show off. “Not one of our markets independently is big enough to turn the tide for Louisiana,” Louisiana’s state economic development CIO Josh Fleig told me this month. The Austin, Dallas and Houston metros next door each rival or exceed the entire state of 4.6 million people. “We have to think of Shreveport, Baton Rouge, Lafayette, New Orleans as one innovation hub, not four.” Likewise, Mayor Morena is part of a new wave of leaders that intend to overcome old tribal battles to reach new solutions. Population decline is a global issue, but it seems too early for a city so treasured. Instead, New Orleans is an enviable tool for Louisiana. Last fall, the national Nasdaq Entrepreneurial Center cited New Orleans entrepreneurs as outperformers. But in a state of fewer than 5 million, smaller than the metro population of adjacent Houston, Texas, its analysis advised a statewide coalition was necessary. New Orleans isn’t a burden the state carries. It’s a superpower only a few states can claim, and its performance is Louisiana’s performance.
impactSentence: Despite ranking among America’s favorite metros, the city is shrinking rapidly while political friction with Baton Rouge stalls a turnaround.

title: How states build innovation coalitions
dek: State agencies, membership groups and informal gatherings: All are wrestling with the same problem — turning rival metros into one connected ecosystem.
body: • Lessons from two states: Louisiana Innovation is a state-agency catalyst; the Arizona Technology Council is a member-funded trade group. Both try to knit competing metros into one statewide ecosystem. • Research shows that networked smaller cities can “borrow size” from bigger neighbors — or fall into an “agglomeration shadow” if the links are weak. • Both states poured the same federal SSBCI dollars overwhelmingly into venture capital, but Louisiana chose a decentralized fund-of-funds, deliberately giving up control. Are you more likely to wear a t-shirt boasting your state, or one with your city? This means something for coalition building. Nationally, two-thirds of us are “proud” of our city or town , per YouGov last year, yet only around half say the same about their state. Like most things, though, there’s real variation across the country. Minnesota, Michigan and Virginia topped the state pride list. Missouri residents were least proud, and surprisingly, Texans statewide pride has declined measurably over the last decade : Now more residents are proud of their city/town than the Lone Star state itself. “There’s a lot more to collaborate about than there is to compete about.” Steven Zylstra, Arizona Tech Council Humans solve problems collectively. To coordinate, we tell stories of identity, threats and opportunity. To attract and retain brainy people to do good work (and dutifully pay taxes), state and local leaders must care a lot about how we feel about where we live, and visit. Last fall, the Nasdaq Entrepreneurial Center ’s annual report argued regional ecosystems ought pay more attention to statewide coalitions .  If states risk devolving into an administrative grouping of rival metros, the question economic developers keep bumping into: who stitches them together, and how? Josh Fleig is Louisiana’s chief innovation officer, running a two-year-old state initiative called Louisiana Innovation . Steven Zylstra is the longtime CEO of the Arizona Technology Council, a member-funded trade group of roughly 750 companies. One works for the governor. The other works for his dues-payers.  Both are trying to turn a handful of competing cities into a single innovation economy and have something to teach the rest of us. import {Runtime, Inspector} from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@observablehq/runtime@5/dist/runtime.js"; import define from "https://api.observablehq.com/d/ff5675b4238a6173.js?v=4"; new Runtime().module(define, name => { if (name === "chart") return new Inspector(document.querySelector("#observablehq-chart-3715a4c2")); }); Place-based leaders must sensibly start with the unique qualities of their jurisdictions, both Zylstra and Fleig agreed.  For slow-growth Louisiana , Fleig said he has a responsibility to develop statewide identity and strategy.  “Not one of our markets independently is big enough to turn the tide for Louisiana,” Fleig said. The Austin, Dallas and Houston metros next door each rival or exceed his entire state of 4.6 million people. “We have to think of Shreveport, Baton Rouge, Lafayette and New Orleans as one innovation hub, not four.” There’s a name for what he’s describing. Urban economists call it “borrowed size” — the idea, traced to a 1973 William Alonso paper, that a smaller city wired into a larger network can access advantages it’s too small to generate alone. The catch, as described in more recent work by Evert Meijers and Martijn Burger, is that weak links produce the opposite: an “agglomeration shadow,” where the small city just gets overlooked. Whether Louisiana’s metros borrow size or sit in a shadow depends on exactly the connective tissue Fleig is trying to build. Zylstra has run this play in two states. Before Arizona, he led the Pittsburgh Technology Council , and he’s a believer in the statewide model with local roots. He’s blunt that the tension never disappears. Smaller cities are “always a little bit envious” of the big metro, he said, and his fix is to staff and program locally — offices in both Phoenix and Tucson, events sprinkled to Flagstaff and Yuma. Both Arizona and his long-ago home of Pennsylvania are states with big cities that have robust identities competing with statewide ones. “There are all kinds of ecosystems — local, regional, statewide and multi-state,” Zylstra said. “There’s no one that’s more important than the other.” You need a statewide coalition to move a legislature; you need a hyper-local one to help a company pick a block. What he refuses is the zero-sum frame: “There’s a lot more to collaborate about than there is to compete about.” Who leads — and who lets go Fleig is adamant that government should catalyze, then step back.  “I philosophically believe this is a free-market thing, and we just need to catalyze areas that might not be working so well but ultimately get out of the way,” he said. It’s the “leaders and feeders” logic that entrepreneurship writers have pushed for a decade — founders lead, institutions feed. Both states have used bits of money to incentive gap-filling and otherwise supported flourishing regional speciality and organizing to come together. For example, SXSW, Austin’s sprawling tech conference turned city-sized activation to hawk products and places, has become a proving ground: Leaders from Alabama, Pennsylvania, Tennessee and Michigan, among others, have all experimented with joint activations. All of them made t-shirt design decisions.  States have access to capital at a scale that no single municipality does. Louisiana and Arizona both dedicate a higher share of federal cash toward equity investments than the national average.  The State Small Business Credit Initiative, the $10 billion program Congress reauthorized in 2021 that’s part of a patchwork of federal funding for high-growth entrepreneurship , is left to states to design. Louisiana was allocated up to $113 million — and rather than run one big state fund, it became a limited partner in about a dozen local seed funds, each required to match with private dollars. Fleig framed the decision as cultural, not financial. A single blue-chip manager “might return more,” he conceded. “But that’s a short-term solution. I’m managing for cultural change.”  His metaphor: “I need a lot of people rowing in the same direction, get more people at the party.” That instinct has academic backing too — economist Josh Lerner’s 2009 Kauffman Foundation-backed “ Boulevard of Broken Dreams ” is a book-length case for why centralized government venture funds tend to fail. Arizona made the same equity bet with a twist that underscores the models’ difference: The state deployed roughly $87 million of its SSBCI money into venture programs through a purpose-built vehicle, the Arizona Venture Development Corporation — not through Zylstra’s council. The trade group convenes and advocates; the state agency writes the checks. Louisiana has earmarked 81% of its allotments toward company equity investing, and Arizona has dedicated 78%, according to our analysis. The national average is closer to a third. import {Runtime, Inspector} from "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@observablehq/runtime@5/dist/runtime.js"; import define from "https://api.observablehq.com/d/1f39ba3d8f9c47d6@39.js?v=4"; new Runtime().module(define, name => { if (name === "chart") return new Inspector(document.querySelector("#observablehq-chart-b038a893")); }); The long game vs. the photo op Both men know the enemy is the calendar.  Economic development “is very much wired and geared to ribbon cutting for big projects,” Fleig said. “Those are immediate wins and they’re very real.” But “grow your own” economic development necessitates an “ecosystem” strategy of many pro-entrepreneurship efforts, at both the grassroots and strategic level, Fleig said. A lot of it fails, he said, but “the 10 or 20% that does has potential to change the future of our economy.” Selling that patience is half the job. Innovation, Fleig told legislators, is not a sideshow but “the beginning of the economic flywheel, the supply chain for the jobs you want later.” The urgency is that federal money is “lumpy,” he said. Unable to depend on a chaotic federal funding landscape (from SSBCI to successive years of federal Tech Hubs and NSF Engines), the work is institutionalizing the strategy “beyond my time.” The Nasdaq Entrepreneurial Center ARIE study, analyzed by Technical.ly, found the strongest startup regions shared “a durable statewide pro-entrepreneurship coalition, reinforced locally.” It also found almost no correlation between a metro’s venture-dollar rank and its actual performance — with capital-scarce New Orleans named as an outperformer. Coalition beats cash. Fleig’s favorite model for the whole thing is a party. Mardi Gras, he said, is “the largest decentralized, unowned, non-corporate party in the world. No one can own it.”  That, more or less, is the ecosystem he’s trying to build — headless, statewide and impossible for any one metro to hoard. title: A summer research program at UMD is preparing students early for the quantum workforce
dek: Frontier Technology Institute is demystifying complex physics with scholarships, stipends and hands-on mentors across the DMV region.
body: This story was made possible through support from TEDCO , the Maryland Technology Development Corporation, which enhances economic empowerment growth through the fostering of an inclusive entrepreneurial innovation ecosystem. TEDCO identifies, invests in, and helps grow technology and life science-based companies in Maryland. Learn more at tedcomd.com . All stories are independently reported, with no partner review. Think you need a Ph.D. to understand quantum technology? Well, the Frontier Technology Institute says otherwise, offering coursework to students as early as high school. The nonprofit introduces young learners to complex physics concepts to build a workforce pipeline as the sector gains steam. Known as Qubit by Qubit , the initiative has trained more than 22,500 students since launching in 2019. Frontier recently capped off its latest summer cohort with a research showcase at the University of Maryland, College Park (UMD), where high school and college participants presented original projects across the quantum, data science and AI fields. A high school student presents her final project to Corey Stambaugh, director of Maryland’s Capital of Quantum Initiative (Maria Eberhart/Technical.ly) “A lot of people hear quantum and think it’s only for geniuses like Einstein,” Frontier CEO Keira Peltz told Technical.ly. “But if we can actually get started early, we can hopefully expand the pool of talent and also change who’s in that pool.” The program aligns with the organization’s broader mission to demystify complex, emerging technologies, Peltz said. Frontier, which rebranded from the Coding School earlier this year, selected the DMV region as its primary quantum hub because of Maryland’s robust investment in the sector. Under Gov. Wes Moore’s “Capital of Quantum” initiative, Maryland is targeting $1 billion in public and private funding to cement its status as an industry hub. Though quantum computing is still inching toward commercial viability in fields like drug discovery and cybersecurity, market data projects that 250,000 quantum jobs will need to be filled by the end of the decade. Practical experience gets a foot in the door Frontier offers virtual classes for its high school research program, pairing students nationwide with live instruction and dedicated research mentors. While tuition for the high school track isn’t cheap — running roughly $4,000 for the summer — grant funding supports 150 full scholarships for students in select states and rural communities.  For undergraduates, the offerings go even deeper. Summer research programs are fully funded for college-aged DMV students interested in cybersecurity and quantum applications. Participants tour quantum companies based at UMD, and students in the six-week early-career track receive a $1,600 stipend, split between training and work at a quantum firm. Real-world experience aims to help students get an early foothold in a competitive industry, according to Peltz. Students involved in the data science and AI tracks also presented at the symposium (Maria Eberhart/Technical.ly) Isai Amaya (second from right) presented his research alongside teammates at the symposium (Maria Eberhart/Technical.ly) “I don’t think it’s fair to train students and say, ‘Hey, work on this game-changing technology, but you have to wait six years to get an internship,’” Peltz said. “It’s a huge accessibility problem.” That approach paid off for one student, Isai Amaya. Before joining the program, the UMD student knew little about the campus’s quantum initiatives beyond the “Capital of Quantum” banners, he said. A cybersecurity professor recommended him for Frontier’s career program, where he collaborated with a mentor at Boston-based QuEra Computing . Now, Amaya plans to pursue quantum and cybersecurity coursework at the university during his senior year.  “This program opened up another world for me,” Amaya said. “I’m really fascinated to see where the future of this technology goes.”
impactSentence: Frontier Technology Institute is demystifying complex physics with scholarships, stipends and hands-on mentors across the DMV region.
