title: A college class on AI became the foundation for this million-acre Louisiana agtech platform
dek: Founder Colin Raby shares the unconventional way he built FarmMind, a Baton Rouge startup serving agriculture businesses.
body: This is How I Got Here , a series where we chart the career journeys of technologists, entrepreneurs, tech workers, builders and people in the innovation economy. Want to tell your story? Get in touch . FarmMind is betting that artificial intelligence can ease one of agriculture’s biggest challenges: finding, understanding and acting on the enormous amount of information behind each growing season. When founder Colin Raby enrolled in a Louisiana State University course on AI and large language models in 2023, the technology was still largely a question mark. Everyone was talking about what AI might change, but fewer knew what to actually build with it. “It’s amazing how fast you can move when you just connect with the right people.” Colin Raby, FarmMind With FarmMind — an LSU spinout based in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, a state where agriculture has a $13 billion economic impact — he’s building an AI-powered platform that brings agricultural research, regulations, field information, documents and other data into one place.  Founded in 2024, its tech is now used across more than 1 million acres , according to the company. It had objectively good timing, launched just as generative AI was taking off .  That timing, however, seems to be less about coincidence and more about Raby’s connections and “just start doing” philosophy. At LSU, he helped create a new AI economic impact course, which connected several of the universities’ schools as they worked on class projects and landed funding to gain momentum.  The path to building that system also took Raby well beyond his engineering background. His experience in student government and as one of Congress’ first AI specialists shaped how he thinks about technology, communication and the incentives that determine whether people actually use the systems they’re given. “The more you can communicate exactly what your goal is, why that’s valuable and then communicate what the incentive is — why this is good for you, why this is good for humanity, why it’s good for the other person,” Raby told Technical.ly, “the more you can rally people into the cause.” In this edition of How I Got Here, Raby talks about the people and circumstances that helped turn FarmMind from an idea into a growing company and why he sees the company as a case study in building momentum without traditional venture capital. This Q&A has been edited for length and clarity. What do you consider to be the beginning of your tech journey? I was always interested in building things, and in high school that was mostly science and engineering. At university, I graduated in engineering, but also ended up getting involved in building non-physical things, whether that be student government stuff, building systems or eventually building companies. FarmMind definitely started in a class at LSU in the fall of 2023 . It was one of the first classes teaching students how to develop economically beneficial systems with large language models. At the time, large language models were very nascent. All the tech people are talking about how this is going to change the world, but like, how do we actually put it to work? We were actually able to recruit someone from Oak Ridge Labs, Professor James Ghawaly , and a local entrepreneur, Henry Hayes , who collaborated with our provost at the time, Roy Haggerty , to put together this first class. It’s amazing how fast you can move when you just connect with the right people. We were able to get a syllabus, get the class approved, everything like that in about three months. I think a lot of people dramatically underestimate the amount of progress you can make if you simply have a bias toward action. Tell me more about starting this class. How did you go about it? What can other people learn from that? We put out a notice to a lot of local businesses and professors at LSU saying, “Come with your ideas of things you would like large language models to do for you.” Come pitch it, and then the students can choose to do that as a project. One of the folks who showed up was Professor Daniel Stephenson of our Ag Center. It was clear there was a huge difference between the information that was out there and the information that people were actually acting on in their agricultural practice. That semester, we worked on this idea of what if we could take all of this LLM technology and make a system specifically for agriculture that thinks like an agricultural professional would think. We had to stall out a little bit after the class just because we didn’t have the resources needed to do it. But fortunately, the first kind of thing that we won was the LSU Venture Challenge in 2024 . That gave us enough money to get a whole AWS server and keep running some experiments. how i got here A college class on AI became the foundation for this million-acre Louisiana agtech platform From biochemistry to venture funding, Fehmida Kapadia is building Maryland’s medtech pipeline How board games and disassembled microwaves led Jason Okerman to found a robotics startup You mentioned the business stalled after a lack of resources. What else helped restart momentum? Louisiana is unfortunately not known for its venture capital networks, and we found that out the hard way. There are a lot of people who will take meetings. Yet when push comes to shove, that’s less true. We ended up going to all these different pitch competitions. We probably only got money from maybe half to a third of the pitch competitions that we went to, but one of the lessons you can learn from a lot of the great stories and people of history is that you are not judged by the quantity of your failures, only by the quality of your success. Nobody ever asks us about the SEC pitch competition that we didn’t even place in. All the focus is on the Louisiana Pelican Cup , the American Farm Bureau Ag Innovation Challenge , and the LSU Venture Challenge wins. They gave us the capital to pay ourselves a meager salary and cover all the expenses, and we were able to get out enough of a prototype to get people using it. Five of our initial users became angel investors. They’re literally users of the thing that decided it was so good they wanted to become investors in it. Whatever you’re selling, get it in the hands of 20 people, and then see if one of them is willing to be an investor. What hurdles did you face, and what’s your advice for others? The biggest hurdle that a lot of builders have in building a business is going from zero to one. There are a million ideas, but very few people can execute on those ideas. Once we were able to go from zero to one, one of our first 10 users actually ended up becoming an angel investor in the company. There are a lot of people who get trapped in planning. It’s like, just start doing. There are way more people who have probably failed with a great plan than people who have just violently executed without a plan and ended up getting really far.
impactSentence: Founder Colin Raby shares the unconventional way he built FarmMind, a Baton Rouge startup serving agriculture businesses.

title: EV motors depend on foreign rare earths. Torev Motors is bringing a potential solution to market.
dek: Following third-party trials in Germany, the Northern Virginia startup is hiring engineers and raising a $5 million seed round.
body: This story was reported with support from our partner Arlington Economic Development , a launchpad for innovation and a top destination for businesses of all sizes. Startup profile: Torev Motors Founded by: Rory Brogan and Zak Doenmez Year founded: 2022 Headquarters: Arlington, VA Sector: EVs, manufacturing Funding and valuation: $3.7M raised to date, valuation not disclosed Key ecosystem partners : Arlington Economic Development, VA Innovation Commercialization Assistance Program As global tensions and supply chain issues create a demand for EV motors that don’t depend on rare earth materials, an Arlington startup just passed the test to begin scaling its solution With third-party testing to make sure the design works for on-road usage, Torev Motors is confident it has proved a version of its flagship product, which swaps out hard-to-source rare earth permanent magnets and instead leverages additional copper coils and electrical steel. The startup is positioning the tech as dual-use , to be deployed in both regular cars and defense vehicles, said cofounder and CEO Rory Brogan.  “We’re still very much in the process of scaling up,” Brogan told Technical.ly. “But we have evidence in hardware that what we’re creating can be a legitimate solution to one of the biggest challenges plaguing the electric motor industry globally right now.” “We have evidence … that what we’re creating can be a legitimate solution to one of the biggest challenges plaguing the electric motor industry globally right now.” Rory Brogan, Torev Motors Right now, the majority of EV motors depend on three kinds of rare earths that are mostly imported from China, which controls more than 99% of processing . Manufacturers of everything from phones to fighter jets are facing supply chain complications for needed rare earths and critical minerals . It’s considered to be a national security for the US. Torev has previously received some support from the federal government to develop its tech for use in military vehicles: a $250,000 a Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) grant. The program, which offers non-dilutive funding for companies, recently lapsed for about six months , leaving an application backlog . It returned with a slew of new rules .  Brogan declined to share information about additional SBIR applications for the program, but noted he was glad Torev Motors’ business model did not rely on that funding.  “Treat the SBIRs as a good thing,” Brogan said. “But not a guarantee.”  Financial growth is accelerating via the private sector, however, with a $5 million seed round on the horizon led by Gula Tech Adventures , a venture firm based in Columbia, Maryland, that focuses on national security technologies. The company also expanded its operational footprint this past summer by opening a dedicated R&D lab in Charlottesville, Virginia, and is actively recruiting engineers and interns to support hardware scaling Three month validation process  Torev Motors’ motor design is flat and small. But with compact designs comes the issue of the tech overheating faster because of its density, Brogan said.  Overheating causes traditional magnet-based motors to shut down entirely. Torev Motors’ architecture instead transfers operational heat to the adhesive surrounding the copper coils rather than causing immediate failure, and is supported by an internal oil cooling system, he said.  Making sure these mechanics work required a three-month testing process that concluded in May, moving from internal stress testing to third-party verification overseas. Future testing will entail making sure the motor meets regulatory and safety requirements . Federal rules don’t technically require independent validation, but major automakers typically don’t buy motors based solely on internal claims.  Internal testing began by balancing the motor on an advanced scale and shaving off excess material. Next, the team performed a burst test to determine the exact speed that would trigger mechanical failure. For Torev Motors, that failure manifested as a hole opening and spraying oil, per Brogan. Torev then shipped the motor to PID , a German third-party testing facility. Rory Brogan of Torev Motors shows off his product at CTI Symposium 2026 (Courtesy) “I wasn’t even in the room, which was one of the most nerve-wracking experiences,” Borgan said. “You hand your baby off to someone and they take it, they close the door, and you just hope that everything works out right.” Engineers measure abilities like speed and torque, handing over data for Torev Motors to compare against its original hypotheses.   “It’s very much like a high school or a college science experiment,” he said.  Following the successful tests, Torev Motors is in talks with automotive commercial companies and plans to deploy its motors in sedans in the next year.  Updated to correct the value of Torev Motors’ SBIR grant.
